metadata.title: OpenClaw Evolutionary Coding Lab: connecting the pieces
metadata.description: Reproducible source, cancellation experiments, and the path to one complete, controlled coding task.

outcome.summary: The source-v9 development snapshot is reproducible and passed its offline checks. New integration work is underway; the complete coding workflow and production qualification remain unfinished.

provenance.summary: AI-assisted project update checked against local source and recorded development validation on September 22, 2026. Engine evidence remains local. The public references document this article and its publication process; they do not independently reproduce the engine results.

blocks.text: OpenClaw Evolutionary Coding Lab is an experimental, locally operated system for carrying out bounded coding tasks. The intended workflow starts with a task and explicit limits, makes changes in an isolated copy of a project, evaluates the result and returns a patch for human review.

The Lab already has project tracking, planning, task scheduling, reporting and mechanisms that control which actions a task may perform. Development fixtures also exercise parts of the execution system. The current challenge is connecting those components into one demonstrable workflow, including what happens when work fails or is stopped.

blocks.label: Current status
blocks.text: A reproducible source snapshot and offline demo are ready for review. Integration has continued since that snapshot, so the next experimental release will need a fresh build and validation. The immediate milestone is one controlled coding task with demonstrated success, failure, restart and cancellation behavior.

blocks.alt: Intended workflow, with integration still in progress: scope and authorize a task with exact source and limits; claim the attempt once and reject replay; run and evaluate changes in an isolated copy; return the patch and test results for human review while preserving the original project.
blocks.caption: Figure 1. The intended workflow. A complete end-to-end demonstration is still pending.

items.label: Source-v9 offline validation
items.value: The extracted snapshot ran 1,587 tests with no unexpected failures or errors. That total includes one expected historical failure; 17 machine-specific checks were excluded.

items.label: Repeatable source export
items.value: Two source exports and a fresh export from the extracted files were byte-for-byte identical. The archive's file hashes and sizes were verified.

items.label: Execution fixtures
items.value: Disposable test programs exercised launch settings, sealed executable data, output limits, deadlines, cleanup within a process group and Windows-to-Linux handoff.

items.label: Release materials
items.value: An installable Python package and synthetic offline demo are prepared, alongside an MIT license, third-party notices, documentation and continuous-integration configuration.

blocks.text: These results apply to specific development artifacts. The offline suite did not rerun the earlier native execution experiments, and the package's demo exercises a synthetic project registry without running coding tasks. The engine source has not yet been published as a GitHub release; the linked portfolio repository hosts this article.

Three executor gaps were reproduced with disposable test processes and corrected. A child closing both output streams no longer disables its deadline. Interrupting capture now stops and reaps the direct child before the original interruption returns to the caller. A pipe held open outside the stopped process group can no longer keep cleanup waiting indefinitely: an incomplete read is reported as an execution error.

That executor snapshot passed a full offline run of 1,591 tests with no unexpected failures, errors or skips. One historical expected failure and 17 explicitly excluded machine-specific checks remain. The tested source hashes were checked at the time of validation. Focused validation also passed 79 checks covering the new regressions and existing execution and one-shot authority behavior.

A separate Windows-to-Linux development fixture also passed two cases after a child and grandchild confirmed they were running: an explicit cancel message, and closure of the input connection. Linux reported the direct child reaped by the executor, the grandchild reaped after termination, and no remaining children. The host observed completion in 247 ms and 211 ms. This is cooperative cancellation evidence for that disposable workload, not proof for forcibly killing the Windows launcher or for descendants that escape containment.

blocks.label: Scope of this result
blocks.text: These corrections are local development changes and are not included in the earlier release-preparation archive. Complete cross-host cancellation, escaped-descendant containment, production qualification and a real coding task remain unfinished.

sections.title: Keeping a result when the requester disappears

blocks.text: Forcibly terminating the Windows requester exposed a gap: the known Linux processes disappeared, but no completion report survived. That experiment remains inconclusive. A separate backend was then tested so the work and its reporting could outlive the requester's connection.

In the latest disposable experiment, Windows terminated the requester after the worker confirmed readiness. The backend detected the disconnect, requested cancellation, confirmed direct-child and grandchild cleanup, and saved a terminal execution-failure result. A separate process reopened the store and read that result. Windows termination took 282 ms; the worker reported completion in 113 ms. These are observations from one experiment, not performance guarantees.

The executor now accepts an explicit cancellation signal and returns a failure observation that the existing task pipeline can save. Focused validation passed 82 execution and authority checks plus a pipeline test showing a persisted failure and no replay launch. A broader pipeline run passed 179 of 182 tests; the other three failed because installed Python or standard-library bytes did not match pinned runtime requirements. Those exact checks were already excluded from the offline profile. Their failures remain unresolved runtime qualification work.

blocks.label: What this establishes
blocks.text: The backend experiment and pipeline regression exercise separate boundaries. They do not yet prove a complete authenticated coding service, service restart recovery, concurrent request handling or containment of escaped descendants. The earlier 1,591-test full-suite result predates explicit cancellation. Current changes are not included in the older release archive.

The explicit-cancellation snapshot subsequently passed a full offline run of 1,595 tests with no unexpected failures, errors or skips. One historical expected failure and 17 named host-dependent exclusions remain. The recorded input hashes still matched after the run. This result predates the recovery adapters described below.

New review-stage code reuses the existing database transaction to save the exact dispatch record when a task is consumed. It can recover that record after a lost response without consuming the task again. A second adapter saves the bound execution evidence and its evaluated outcome together, then re-evaluates that evidence when the store is reopened. It accepts no caller-selected verdict.

Seventeen targeted checks passed across the recovery and cancellation work. Separate-process tests showed that conflicting valid outcomes have one winner, identical submissions create only one terminal transition, and a result survives an abrupt process exit immediately after commit. Other checks reject incomplete or forged evidence and preserve failed-test and execution-failure outcomes.

blocks.label: Component recovery, not service qualification
blocks.text: These adapters use synthetic witness evidence and are not connected to production task dispatch. The existing transport contract still requires a root-owned systemd socket and authenticated deployment identities. Accepted runtime and policy setup, authenticated witness delivery, one-use execution claims and complete workflow recovery remain unfinished. The older release archive does not include these changes.

blocks.alt: Three stages of progress: the verified source-v9 snapshot has a repeatable source export and offline checks; current development tests cancellation and integration with focused checks; the next demonstration must complete one isolated coding task through success, failure, restart and cancellation. Production qualification remains open.
blocks.caption: Figure 2. The verified snapshot, current integration work and next demonstration are separate milestones.

blocks.text: The remaining work connects authenticated task delivery, a protected execution identity and the final runtime environment. Stopping a task must also stop the work it started, with evidence covering child processes, interrupted callers and the Windows-to-Linux boundary.

The proposed policy changes still need acceptance, and the actual runtime still needs qualification: checks that the intended executable, libraries, permissions and launch conditions are enforced together. Passing component tests does not establish those properties for a live coding task.
The evolutionary part also has a clear limit today. The current convergence process uses a population of one. Broader search across multiple competing candidates remains future work.

items.title: Extend stopping and recovery evidence
body: Build on the demonstrated cleanup and cancellation paths. Resolve escaped-descendant containment and verify service restart recovery and concurrent request handling through the complete workflow, with bounded behavior and durable results.

items.title: Connect the existing authority chain
body: Bind the task, exact source, permitted actions and deadline to the protected runtime and isolated workspace. The existing broker already rejects replayed task consumption; demonstrate that lost responses and restarts cannot trigger a second execution through the complete workflow.

items.title: Complete one real coding task
body: Use an isolated copy of a small test project. Capture a proposed patch and its test results while preserving the original. Demonstrate success, a deliberate test failure, replay or restart handling, and cancellation.

items.title: Build a fresh experimental release
body: Rebuild from the updated source, repeat installation in a clean environment and validate the new export. Publish reproducible instructions with a precise account of the demonstrated capabilities and remaining limits.

blocks.text: Each update will identify the artifact or source state behind its results, describe failures as well as successes, and separate implemented behavior from planned capabilities. Progress toward a complete coding workflow will be measured by demonstrated behavior, including recovery and stopping. Public updates summarize the findings without exposing private logs, local paths or internal authority records.
